newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open stronger on tame U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open stronger on tame U.S. data.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened stronger on Thursday as a tame U.S. retail sales report for May reduced expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike rates in July, analaysts said.

"Today's numbers really did suggest that weakness that we were all expecting to creep into the economy is starting to happen. That's portending no move from the Fed," said Walter Posiewko, a money market trader with Royal Bank Investment Management.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 2.93 percent from 2.94 percent at Wednesday's close.
Both Canadian and U.S. fixed-income markets strengthened after the U.S. Commerce Department reported that retail sales fell 0.1 percent in May, compared with expectations of a 0.4 percent rise.

"Now you're seeing guys on a Thursday settlement date that need bills just rushing in and getting them out," said Posiewko. "I don't think the account base is buying it down here. I think more likely you're seeing shorts being covered on the street as the result of the strength in the market. It's all U.S.-driven."
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.20 percent from 3.27 percent. The one-year T-bill firmed to yield 3.77 percent from 3.84 percent.

The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.10 percent, in the upper half of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range. Dealers said the rise is the call loan rate was linked settlement pressures from Tuesday's weekly T-bill auction.
